title: Buttercream chrysanthemum piping
subtitle: a piped flower built from short narrow petals layered outward from a central mound
excerpt: A buttercream chrysanthemum is a piped flower built from short, narrow petals laid outward in rings from a central mound of buttercream. It is piped onto a flower nail using a petal nozzle and transferred to the cake once all the layers are complete. The flower looks most natural in two slightly different tones of the same colour.
sourceNotes: Chrysanthemum piping technique found in American cake-decorating manuals from the mid-twentieth century onward, widely taught in British sugarcraft from the 1970s.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small rotating metal nail used as a platform when building piped buttercream or royal icing flowers. The nail is held in one hand and turned while the piping bag works with the other.

content.text: A buttercream chrysanthemum is a piped flower built ring by ring from short, curved petals. It is made on a
and transferred to the cake with an icing spatula. The petal nozzle is held with the narrow end pointing outward, and each petal is made with a short press-and-pull of the bag while the nail rotates.
The buttercream must be stiff enough to hold a peak but soft enough to move through the nozzle without cracking. Chill the piping bag for 10 minutes if the kitchen is warm.
Place a small square of baking paper on the flower nail and secure it with a tiny dot of buttercream. The paper makes the flower easy to lift off without damage.
Fit the piping bag with the petal nozzle. The nozzle has one narrow end and one wide end. Hold the bag so the wide end of the nozzle touches the centre of the nail and the narrow end points outward.
Pipe the centre: press out a small mound of buttercream in the middle of the nail. This is the base the petals build from.

For the inner ring, rest the wide end of the nozzle against the side of the centre mound. Apply pressure and pull the bag outward about 1 cm, then release. This makes one short, curved petal standing upright. Rotate the nail slightly and repeat to fill the ring with 6 to 8 petals.

For the middle ring, angle the nozzle slightly more outward (about 45 degrees from vertical). Pipe petals that are a little longer than the inner ring and lay outward. Add 10 to 12 petals in this ring.

For the outer ring, hold the nozzle nearly horizontal. Pipe longer petals that spread out flat around the base of the flower. This ring fills in the edge and gives the chrysanthemum its full, rounded silhouette.
Slide an icing spatula beneath the baking paper and transfer the flower to the cake or to a tray lined with baking paper. Chill for 20 minutes to firm before placing.

attrs.problem: Petals collapsing rather than standing upright
attrs.avoid: Avoid soft or warm buttercream; the petals will not hold their angle.
attrs.fix: Chill the filled piping bag for 15 minutes before piping. The cooler buttercream holds the shape of each petal as it comes out of the nozzle.

attrs.problem: Petals cracking and breaking as they come out of the nozzle
attrs.avoid: Avoid buttercream that is too cold or too stiff; it will split under the pressure of squeezing.
attrs.fix: Let the piping bag warm up in your hands for a minute before piping. The heat from your palms softens the buttercream slightly.

attrs.problem: Flower falling apart when transferred from the nail
attrs.avoid: Avoid transferring while the buttercream is still very soft; the petals will shift.
attrs.fix: Place the entire nail in the freezer for 5 minutes after piping. The cold firms the flower so it holds together when you slide the spatula underneath.
